## Towards the Robustness of Multiple Object Tracking Systems

Xiaoyuan Xie ∗ † , Ying Duan ∗ , Songqiang Chen ∗ † , Jifeng Xuan ∗ ∗ School of Computer Science, Wuhan University, China

xxie@whu.edu.cn, duan ying@whu.edu.cn, i9schen@gmail.com, jxuan@whu.edu.cn

Abstract -Due to the wide use of visual perception techniques in safety-critical fields, existing studies have tested the robustness of the essential object detection systems in scenarios with different image content. However, the applications that perceive one video with multiple image frames, such as autonomous driving, usually further require the trajectories of objects. This is mainly realized by combining detecting objects and associating detected objects in frames using multiple object tracking (MOT) systems. Thus, it is also essential to test the robustness of MOT systems, particularly in their exclusive scenarios that involve variety beyond the static image content. In this paper, we propose a novel testing method with five new Metamorphic Relations to realize the robustness test for MOT systems in two typical categories of scenarios, i.e., the speed variety of tracked objects and temporary camera failures. Our method also properly addresses the oracle problem and the lack of test cases for some rare scenarios to make the test efficient and diverse. Finally, we use our method to test three typical MOT systems and effectively reveal numerous and diverse MOT errors. We also extensively discuss the performance of tested systems and summarize two typical scenes where they often misbehave.

Index Terms -multiple object tracking, robustness, metamorphic testing, deep learning testing, autonomous driving testing

## I. I NTRODUCTION

Considering the wide use of the visual perception techniques in many safety-critical applications, existing works have tested the robustness of the image object detection (OD) systems [1][3], which perform as an essential beginning part in the visual perceptual pipeline. But in the visual perceptual pipeline for a video with multiple image frames, which is also widely-used in various fields like autonomous driving, the detected objects in every frame are further associated into several trajectories. This complete process is called as Multiple Object Tracking (MOT). For example, one autonomous vehicle usually equips with an MOT system to track the obstacles, based on which the later move of obstacles is predicted and the future driving path of vehicle is planned [4]. As a result, the error of MOT systems will also disturb these applications and cause accidents [5], [6]. Thus, for the critical applications on video, solely studying the robustness of OD systems is insufficient. It is also essential to evaluate the robustness of MOT systems in diverse scenarios. 1 However, no work has studied the robustness of MOT systems in diverse scenarios with an efficient testing method yet.

Since MOT may involve OD, they do share some scenarios that touch the variety on static image content, e.g., with unique brightness or being partially covered somewhere. As such, the

† Co-corresponding authors.

1 In this paper, the robustness of the visual perception systems refers to their performance consistency on the test cases with diverse features, e.g., different weather conditions, object moving speeds, etc., following early works [7], [8].

robustness issues of MOT systems under these scenarios might have been simultaneously revealed in testing OD systems in an application. But MOT systems have a few exclusive scenarios involving some dynamic features like the speed of the tracked objects. These scenarios are also vital and can closely relate to a few accidents. For example, we have usually heard of the autonomous driving system fails when an autonomous vehicle moves fast (and the relative speed of tracked obstacle varies ), ending by a fatal crash [9], [10]. As such, it is of a great need to study the robustness of MOT systems, particularly in those unstudied scenarios that involve dynamic features, with the expectation to reveal some unaware robustness defects .

However, it is not easy to extensively test the robustness of MOT systems in diverse scenarios because of two challenges. On one hand, testing the MOT systems encounters the oracle problem . Currently, the test oracles (reference labels) for the MOT test cases require manual annotation. Furthermore, there can be many frames in a video, as well as many objects in each frame. Some objects of the same type could closely resemble each other as well. These make the annotation workload both heavy and tough. Thus, albeit abundant videos can be collected for testing MOT systems, these cases are usually unusable for an extensive and efficient test due to the lack of easily obtained test oracles. On the other hand, it is not that easy to prepare the test cases of some rare scenarios . More specifically, some temporary unexpected scenarios, such as the short-time image blur, could also disturb MOT systems [11]. These scenarios are inevitable. Actually, they should be more seriously considered, precisely because they are fairly rare corner cases. But the test cases of such scenarios are hard to collect, as these scenarios are rare in the daily use of MOT systems. Lacking these cases has the test incomplete and less diverse. Both challenges keep us from the extensive robustness test for MOT systems.

In this paper, we propose a testing method to well address the above challenges and enable the both efficient and diverse robustness test for MOT systems, particularly in two categories of unstudied scenarios that involve the speed variety of tracked objects and the temporary camera failures. Specifically, we use Metamorphic Testing (MT) [12] and design five Metamorphic Relations (MRs) to generate new (follow-up) test cases from the existing (source) test cases by considering the variety about some dynamic features. The MRs also define an output relation that a robust MOT system should follow on each pair of source and follow-up cases. Next, we execute the tested MOT system on each pair of test cases and inspect the output relation against MRs. Once the MR is violated, a robustness issue in a specific scenario is revealed. This testing method does not require the reference labels of test cases thus addresses the first challenge. And it can generate test cases for a few scenarios, including the rare scenarios like camera failures, to test MOT systems under the rare scenarios therefore well tackles the second challenge.

To evaluate our method, we use it to test three typical MOT systems. Results suggest that our method can effectively reveal numerous and diverse MOT errors. Actually, for all these three test objects, we have detected MOT errors with over two thirds of test case pairs of any MR, which shows the great robustness defects in current MOT techniques. We next extensively study the revealed defects at the granularity of frames and errors, as well as compare the strengths and weaknesses of test objects. Finally, we also summarize two representative scenes in which the test objects often fail. We hope our extensive analysis could inspire the improvement of MOT systems.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

- We propose a method to test the robustness of a new kind of visual perception systems, namely MOT systems. This method also effectively addresses the oracle problem and the lack of test cases for some rare scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, it is the fi rst method to efficiently test the robustness of MOT systems in diverse scenarios.
- We design five Metamorphic Relations (MRs) to simulate five unstudied visual scenarios involving dynamic feature, aiming to reveal unaware robustness defects . Two MRs are for two specific scenarios about the speed variety of tracked objects. The other three MRs are for three specific scenarios about the temporary camera failures.
- We adopt our method to test three typical MOT systems. Extensive results demonstrate that our method can effectively reveal numerous and diverse MOT errors. We also discuss the performance of three test objects in depth, as well as summarize two scenes in which they often fail, in the hope of inspiring the improvement of MOT systems.

The rest of this paper goes as follows. Section II introduces the MOT technique and our motivation to test MOT systems. Section III elaborates our testing method and five Metamorphic Relations. After that, Sections IV and V present the setup and the results of our evaluation experiments, respectively. Next, Sections VI and VII discuss the threats to validity and related works. Finally, Section VIII concludes this paper.

The replication package of this paper is available at [13].

## II. B ACKGROUND AND M OTIVATION

## A. Multiple Object Tracking

Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) aims to recognize multiple objects and trace their trajectories in a video with many image frames. Given a video, an MOT system detects objects in each frame and assigns ID to each detected object in all frames. All the detected objects in a frame will be assigned with different IDs. The detected objects with the same ID across the frames in the whole video will formulate one trajectory. For example, in Fig. 1, MOT systems will identify two trajectories (for the detected objects with IDs of 1 and 2, respectively) in this way.

Fig. 1: Illustration for Multiple Object Tracking

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Specifically, let us denote a video with multiple frames as V = f 1 , . . . , f n , where f i is the i -th frame in V . Given V , the MOT system returns an MOT result of V , which is denoted as T = { T 1 , . . ., T n } , where T i = { ( o i, 1 , id i, 1 ) , . . ., ( o i,m , id i,m ) } is the tracking result on f i ; while o i,j and id i,j are the location and assigned ID of the j -th detected object in f i , respectively. As such, given an ID r , all the detected objects in V that are assigned with r formulate a trajectory, which is denoted with a vector J r = ( o p 1 ,q 1 , id p 1 ,q 1 ) , . . . , ( o pk,qk , id pk,qk ) , where id pi,qi = r , ( o pi,qi , id pi,qi ) ∈ T pi , 1 ≤ p 1 &lt;...&lt;pk ≤ n . And we collect all trajectories formulated in V into J = { J 1 , . . . , J l } . Thus, the trajectories identified in Fig. 1 are J = { J 1 , J 2 } , in which J 1 consists of two detected objects marked in the green boxes in f 1 and f 2 ; while J 2 consists of three detected objects marked in the orange boxes in f 1 , f 2 , and f 3 .

As a reminder, those IDs are merely used to associate the detected objects that are recognized as the same entity across video and formulate a trajectory. When judging the correctness of an MOT result, the practitioners only consider whether the formulated trajectories are consistent with the reference, but no need to consider the absolute value of the ID of each trajectory [14], [15]. For example, in Fig. 1, the absolute ID value in either trajectory would not affect the correctness of the MOT results. It is also reasonable to assign the IDs of 1 and 2 to the detected objects in the orange and green boxes, respectively. In this paper, we follow this principle to design our violation measurement method as well.

Current MOT systems mainly follow three paradigms. Most of them are in the Tracking by Dectection paradigm [16]-[20]. Such MOT systems are with a two-stage workflow, i.e., object detection and object association. Specifically, they first use an object detection system [21]-[24] to detect objects within all frames in the video. Each detected object is identified with one bounding box and one type. In the second stage, these MOT systems predict the relation among the detected objects across frames and assign IDs to associate all the detected objects that are recognized as belonging to the same entity based on their own bounding box and type. Afterward, as introduced above, all the detected objects with the same ID formulate a trajectory. The second paradigm of MOT systems is known as Tracking by Segmentation [25]-[27]. The only difference between such MOTsystems and the previous ones is that these MOT systems adopt one instance segmentation system [28], [29] rather than the object detection system. This helps to locate the border of each object in a more precise manner, such that there would not be overlap among the detected objects to disturb the object association. Another paradigm of MOT systems is called Joint Detection and Tracking [30]-[32]. Such MOT systems have a neural model to accomplish both the object detection and the object association jointly, so as to save the computational cost and time accumulated in two individual stages. This is realized by building and training specific neural network models. In this paper, we use our method to test three typical MOT systems that belong to the above three paradigms, respectively.

## B. Motivation

MOT systems play an important role in many safety-critical applications. A representative field is autonomous driving [4][6]. They are also widely used in critical areas such as security monitoring [33], [34], traffic analysis [35], [36], and pedestrian tracking [37], [38]. As a result, MOT systems are desired to maintain good robustness against tracking performance in diverse scenarios [7], such that the whole critical application can keep running stably. For example, the MOT system within the autonomous car is desired to correctly track obstacles when the car drives at any proper speed and the relative speed of the tracked obstacles varies, as well as after some temporary image blurring, so as to keep the car running stably in these scenarios. By contrast, the poor robustness of MOT systems may disturb the run and harm the reliability of critical applications, thereby pose serious threats to public safety.

In fact, several non-robust tracking-related phenomena have been seen in a few applications with MOT systems. Consider autonomous driving as one example. Several UAV users report that their UA Vs would lose tracked targets after the camera temporarily jumps out of focus or suffers barrel distortion [11], [39]. Moreover, a few fatal accidents have occurred to autonomous cars. According to a survey from the AUTOPILOT REVIEW website [10], one of the most common causes for the crashes of the Tesla Autopilot car is 'hitting stationary objects at freeway speeds'. These cars are particularly likely to miss obstacles when driving at a speed over 80 km/h . In addition, a few tragedies on autonomous cars are also blamed for their failures to detect and track obstacles in diverse scenarios [9], [40], [41]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to reveal the robustness issues of MOT systems in various scenarios.

As mentioned in Section I, there exist a few MRs for visual perception systems to evaluate their robustness against changes on static features. However, we found that the non-robust MOT phenomena are often concerning the variety of some dynamic features, e.g., the speed of tracked objects and the occurrence of camera failures as above. These scenarios have been barely considered in existing works and the relevant defects cannot be detected with existing MRs. Thus, in this work, we mainly focus on the robustness of MOT systems in these scenarios and hope to supplement the existing MRs and reveal the essential yet unaware defects in these unexplored scenarios.

## III. M ETHODOLOGY

## A. Overview of the Testing Method

As mentioned in Section I, it faces two challenges to extensively test the robustness of MOT systems, namely the oracle problem and the lack of the test cases for some rare scenarios. Metamorphic Testing (MT) is a method to effectively address the oracle problem and reuse the existing test cases to generate new test cases based on several properties of tested software, which are known as Metamorphic Relations (MRs) [12], [42].

Fig. 2: Overview of Our Testing Method

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Thus, in this work, we use MT along with five MRs on five specific MOT scenarios to test the robustness of MOT systems in these scenarios. These five MRs generate new test cases to mimic the scenarios that involve the variety on two categories of dynamic features, i.e., the speed of tracked objects and the occasional occurrence of camera failure, and require the tested MOT system to robustly return consistent tracking results. The violations to MRs will reveal the errors in tracking results on the executed test cases, as well as imply the robustness defects of the tested MOT system in corresponding scenarios.

Fig. 2 illustrates the overview of our method. Specifically, given one existing video V (also known as a source test case), we first adopt an MR to generate a new video V (also known as a follow-up test case) with a transformation over a dynamic feature (e.g., speeding up tracked objects). Next, we run MOT system under test (SUT) on both videos and collect the output tracking results T and T for V and V , respectively. We then check the consistence between T and T against the MR. Once the MR is violated, at least one of T and T includes an error and a robustness defect of SUT is revealed. The transformation and the violation detection of the proposed MRs are elaborated in Sections III-B and III-C, respectively.

This method effectively enables the desired robustness test for MOT systems. On one hand, it does not require the MOT labels for test cases. As a result, abundant videos can be easily used, regardless the existence of labels, to test MOT systems. On the other hand, we can design MRs to generate test cases of rare scenarios, so as to supplement the existing test suits. This enriches the test in those rare scenarios and helps to reveal the robustness issues that cannot be revealed by current test suits.

## B. Metamorphic Relations

In this work, we design five novel MRs to test the robustness of MOT systems. These MRs particularly simulate two scenarios, i.e., the ordinary speed variety of tracked objects and the rare unexpected camera failures. They creatively focus on the variety of some dynamic features by transforming the relation of frames instead of solely modifying the static image content. In this section, we illustrate the scenarios these MRs simulate and how they generate the new test cases of each scenario.

1) MRs on the Speed Variety of Tracked Objects: A robust MOT system should correctly track the objects moving at any speed 2 . For example, the MOT system in an autonomous car should correctly track both high- and low-speed obstacles. And it should also work well when the car runs at any proper speed. Therefore, we design two MRs to test the robustness of MOT systems in tracking objects with different speeds (to camera).

Since a video consists of a series of images captured by the camera at a fixed frame rate, one object would be captured in fewer frames if it goes an equal distance at a faster speed. This inspires us to remove frames from the existing video to mimic the speed up of tracked objects. In this paper, we design two MRs that take two removing strategies to mimic a stable high speed and some slight speed waves, respectively.

## MR1-1: Extracting the frames at a fixed interval of k to simulate the stable k -time speed of tracked objects.

MR1-1 mimics the situation where the tracked objects stably move at a k -time speed than in the original video. Specifically, given one video V = f 1 , . . . , f n , MR1-1 extracts the frames at a interval of k and removes the other frames to formulate one new video V = f 1 , . . . , f m . The mapping between the frames in V and V is defined as:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Since the speed variety would not affect traces, the trajectories formulated (on mapped frames) in V and V should be same. Therefore, we require the tracking result T i of any frame f i in V to be consistent to the tracking result T ik of its mapped frame f ik in V (Section III-C1 elaborates the rationale for this transfer). Fig. 3(a) shows an example of MR1-1 where k is 2.

## MR1-2: Randomly removing p % frames to simulate the slight speed waves for tracked objects.

MR1-2 mimics the situation where some slight speed waves occur to the tracked objects in the original video. Specifically, given a video V = f 1 , . . . , f n , MR1-2 randomly removes a few ( p % ) frames (whose indexes are denoted as q 1 , . . . , q r in ascending order) from V and collects the remained frames to formulate a new video V = f 1 , . . . , f m . The frame mapping from V to V is defined as:

Similar to MR1-1, we require the tracking result on any frame remained in V to be consistent with the result on the mapped frame in V . Fig. 3(b) presents an example of this MR where one frame f q is removed.

2) MRs on the Occasional Temporary Camera Failures: In the practical use, MOT systems may inevitably receive some frames with slight unexpected disturbance, such as the blurred or distorted image caused by the occasional camera failures as Section II-B mentions. Even appearing rarely and often lasting for a short term, such invalid content may affect MOT systems processing the other normal frames. Therefore, MOT systems are desired to robustly handle the subsequent normal frames without being affected by the temporary invalid image content.

Fig. 3: Illustration for the Five Proposed MRs

In this paper, we design three MRs to study the robustness of MOT systems against three common camera failures, i.e., the video freeze, signal jamming, and focus loss. It is worth noting that they enrich the testing for MOT systems in these camerafailure scenarios whose existing test cases are fairly rare.

## MR2-1: Randomly covering p % frames with their own previous frames to simulate the occasional video freeze.

MR2-1 mimics the situation of the occasional video freeze. Similar to MR1-2, for a video V = f 1 , . . . , f n , MR2-1 picks a few ( p % ) frames (whose indexes are denoted as q 1 , . . . , q r in ascending order) from V randomly. Next, it covers the picked frames using their respective previous frames to formulate one new video V = f 1 , . . . , f m . And the frame mapping is as:

As the temporary invalid content caused by occasional camera failures should not affect the trajectories formulated across the normal frames, it requires the tracking result on any uncovered frame in V (i.e., f i , i = q j and 1 ≤ j ≤ r ) to be consistent with the result on its mapped frame in V . One example of this MR is presented in Fig. 3(c), where one frame f q is covered.

MR2-2: Randomly pixelating p % frames to simulate the occasional signal jamming.

## MR2-3: Randomly blurring p % frames to simulate the camera losing focus.

Both MR2-2 and MR2-3 are similar with MR2-1 in general. The only difference is the two MRs replace the picked frames with their pixelated and blurred versions, respectively, instead of their respective previous frames that MR2-1 uses. The frame mapping for MR2-2 and MR2-3 is defined as:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

We implement MR2-2 and MR2-3 using the pixel substitution operation following [43] and gaussian blurring following [44], respectively. Both of them have been adopted to simulate realworld corruptions [45], [46]. And we also require the tracking results on any non-pixelated/non-blurred frame to be consistent with that of its mapped frames in V . Figs. 3(d) and 3(e) are the corresponding examples for these two MRs where one frame f q is pixelated/blurred.

Besides, as MR1-2, MR2-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3 randomly modify p % frames to generate follow-up videos, given a source video and one specified p , they can generate multiple distinct follow-up videos to effectively reveal tracking issues. As such, we use them to generate multiple ( q in total) different followup videos for each source video. If the output relation between a source video and any of its q follow-up videos violates the MR, we report it as a violation detected with this source video.

## C. Detection and Description of Violations

As mentioned in Section III-B, our MRs require the trajectories formulated in each pair of source and follow-up videos to be consistent. In this section, we first introduce the method to detect the violation to MRs based on the consistence between the tracking results on the mapped frames in these two videos. Next, we present how we will analyze the test results, i.e., the detected violations and inconsistence, in three granularities.

1) Consistence Measurement for Formulated Trajectories: As mentioned above, given the tracking results on a pair of source and follow-up videos, we need to measure if consistent trajectories can be formulated according to the tracking results for this pair of videos. Recall that the accuracy measurement for MOT systems also aims to inspect the consistence between two sets of trajectories, i.e., the formulated trajectories and the reference trajectories, and it is accomplished by comparing the output tracking result to the reference tracking result on every frame [14], [15]. Inspired by this, in our method, we propose comparing the tracking results on each pair of unchanged mapped frames in source and follow-up videos , in order to measure the consistence between the trajectories formulated in these two videos and judge the violation to MRs. Focusing on the unchanged mapped frames gives us two tracking result sequences with the same length to compare. Now we can easily judge whether the tracking results violate an MR following the measurement of accuracy for MOT systems. Following [14], [15], we measure consistence from two aspects, i.e., the object detection consistence and the ID assignment consistence .

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

MissingDetection

Fig. 4: Illustration for Detected Inconsistence and Errors

For object detection consistence , we examine if the detected objects in any two mapped frames can be one-to-one matched exactly according to their locations. Specifically, given T i and T j , i.e., the tracking results of a frame f i in follow-up video V and its mapped frame f j in source video V , respectively, for every o j,q in T j , we measure its IoU 3 with all o i,p in T i . The detected object at o j,q in f j is matched to the detected object which has a maximum IoU (denoted as ε ) with it in f i when ε is greater than 0.5. Finally, once there is any detected object in f i or f j cannot be matched, the two tracking results are seen as inconsistent regarding the object detection. Taking the case in Fig 4 as an example, a car is detected in f j (marked in green box) but cannot be matched to any object detected in the mapped f i ; an object is detected in f i (marked in yellow box) but cannot be matched to any object detected in the mapped f j . For either case, the MR is violated on this pair of videos.

2) Granularities of Test Result: As introduced above, once any inconsistence about object detection or ID assignment is

For ID assignment consistence , we further check if any two detected objects (in two mapped frames f i and f j ), which are matched with each other in previous step, formulate consistent trajectories. Specifically, given T i and T j , for any two matched objects respectively detected at o i,p in f i of V and at o j,q in f j of V , we use their assigned IDs, id i,p and id j,q , to find their associated trajectories, J x and J y , where x = id i,p and y = id j,q . Next, following the MOT accuracy measurement [14], [15], we inspect the consistence between J x and J y just before f i and f j (based on f i and f j and their respective previous frames). If there is inconsistence identified, then T i and T j are deemed as inconsistent regarding their ID assignment. Taking the case in Fig 4 as an example, in one frame f i and its mapped frame f j , the detected red car is assigned with two IDs, i.e., 2 and 4, respectively (as a reminder, as introduced in Section II-A, this does not mean their trajectories are inconsistent, as long as in previous frame f i -1 and its mapped frame f j -1 this red car is respectively assigned with 2 and 4 as well). However, in f i -1 and f j -1 , this car is assigned with 2 and 3, respectively. Now, it means this red car is associated into inconsistent trajectories in f i and f j . The MR is thereby violated on this pair of videos. This phenomenon is known as an ID switch in f i [14], [15].

3 Intersection-over-Union (IoU) measures the overlap of two object detection bounding boxes for the detection-based MOT systems or two object segmentation masks for the segmentation-based MOT systems.

detected in the tracking results on a pair of source and followup videos, the tested MOT system (SUT) is regarded to violate the MR on this pair of test cases. In this manner, we can easily report the detected robustness issues at a granularity of videos (test cases). However, such granularity may be too coarse and keep us away from the specific findings on SUT's robustness. Thus, in this work, we introduce three granularities, i.e., video level, frame level, and specific error level, to describe the test results, which help us gradually dive into the test results.

Video Level. For test result at this level, we report on how many video pairs SUT violates MRs, i.e., the tracking results on at least a pair of mapped frames are inconsistent. This tells to what extent SUT cannot be totally robust on the video pairs.

Frame Level. It is too coarse to merely investigate if SUT makes any error in a pair of videos. For example, it is unwise to consider an SUT that fails to track objects in 1 second (a few frames) is as robust as another SUT that fails to track objects across all the frames in a video. Therefore, we also report the detected inconsistence in a frame level, that is, in how many pairs of mapped frames the inconsistence is identified for SUT. We regard this amount as the 'violation strength' of SUT on a pair of videos. It tells to what extent (e.g., how long) the SUT is non-robust on each pair of videos in a specific scenario.

Specific Error Level. As the consistence is judged against each detected object, we go further to report how many specific inconsistence errors are identified. Moreover, since there are multiple types of inconsistence, we can go further to identify the type of each error. Following the taxonomy of MOT errors [14], [15], we consider three types of MOT errors, i.e., missing detection, additional detection, and ID switch. Fig. 4 shows the examples for these errors, which have already been concretely introduced in Section III-C1. Such specific information would tell how SUT misbehaves when its robustness defects appear.

## IV. E XPERIMENTAL S ETUP

## A. Research Questions

We evaluate our method along following research questions:

- RQ1: The Overall Effectiveness of Our Method. In this RQ, we investigate whether our method can detect violations to MRs for three typical MOT systems.
- RQ2: Details of the Detected Violations. Since the detected violations can be analyzed in two finer granularities, i.e., frame level and error level, in this RQ, we further investigate the number of the frames including errors and the number of the detected errors in each type.
- RQ3: Comparison among Different MOT Systems. In this RQ, we compare and discuss the robustness of the three tested MOT systems based on our test results.
- RQ4: Summarization of Error-Prone Scenes. In this RQ, we aim to summarize common scenes where three test objects often misbehave by manually reviewing the detected errors, with the expectation to provide some specific directions for improving MOT systems.

## B. Test Cases

In this work, we use the videos in the test set of a popular MOT dataset, KITTI tracking [47], as the source test cases. It includes 29 videos of real-world road scenes captured by the onboard camera of running cars. We use our MRs to generate the corresponding follow-up test cases for every source test case, during which the parameter k for MR1-1 is set as 2 to simulate the double speed; p and q for the other four MRs are set to be 1 and 5, respectively, to generate five new videos with different occasional slight disturbance. Besides, when adopting the four MRs that pick random frames to modify, we prepare the same follow-up test cases for all test objects.

## C. Test Objects

We use three typical MOT systems as our test objects:

SORT+YOLOv3 is a typical Tracking by Detection MOT model combination. SORT [16] is an algorithm to associate the objects detected by an external object detector while YOLOv3 [24] is one popular efficient object detection model. Following [16], we train a YOLOv3 model with the training set of KITTI tracking and combine it to SORT to formulate an MOT system for KITTI. We use this system as the test object.

PointTrack [27] is a typical Tracking by Segmentation MOT system. It first uses an integrated instance segmentation model to extract objects in each frame of a video. Next, it associates the objects across frames to formulate trajectories. The authors of PointTrack have released one official version of PointTrack for KITTI. We load this implementation as the test object.

CenterTrack [32] is a typical Joint Detection and Tracking MOT system. It has one specific neural model to jointly detect and associate objects in each frame based on the image content and the heat map of frames. There is also an officially released version of CenterTrack for KITTI. We also load this released implementation as the test object.

## V. R ESULTS AND A NALYSIS

## A. The Overall Testing Effectiveness (RQ1)

To study the overall effectiveness of our method, we report the number of the source videos with which we successfully detect violations using each MR. For MR1-2, MR2-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3, as we introduce in Section III-B, once the output relation between one source video and any of its five follow-up videos generated with these MRs violates the MRs, we report it as one violtaion detected with this source video.

Table I shows the test result. From the result, we found that any of the five MRs successfully detects violations for all three test objects. This demonstrates that our method and MRs can effectively detect the tracking errors and reveal the robustness defects for three test objects. Moreover, we surprisingly notice that all the three test objects make tracking errors in over twothirds (20) tests under any MR. In several tests, e.g., MR1-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3 for CenterTrack, we detect violations even in all tests. On one hand, this demonstrates that our method and MRs can effectively reveal quite a few defects of MOT systems . On the other hand, it reminds us that existing MOT systems , which may have shown a fairly good performance in the benchmark-based evaluation, can still conceal numerous and diverse robustness issues . Thus, there is an urgent need to extensively test the robustness of the MOT systems across diverse scenarios, in order to protect those critical applications that involve MOT systems from being harmed by the unaware MOT robustness defects.

We also preliminarily compare the performance of three test objects in different scenarios. Regard that all MRs detect quite a few violations. This demonstrates that the robustness of three test objects struggles with both the stable variety mimicked by MR1-1 and the occasional variety simulated by the other four MRs. And they make slightly more errors under MR1-1, which mimics a stable status but also involves more modification on the source video. In addition, judging from the type of dynamic features that each MR transforms, we found that the three test objects tend to make more errors when the speed of the tracked objects varies (MR1-1 and MR1-2) than after the camera fails for a short while (MR2-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3).

## B. Detailed Investigation on Detected Violations (RQ2)

According to the test results at video level reported in RQ1, the test objects do not express much difference of robustness in different scenarios (MRs). Therefore, in this RQ, we go deeper and investigate the robustness of these test objects with finer test results as introduced in Section III-C2. And as a reminder, in this section, we mainly focus on the general findings about three test objects under different MRs. The comparison among the performance of test objects will be presented in RQ3.

We first analyze the test results at frame level . Specifically, we investigate the amount of the mapped frame pairs in which inconsistence is detected. This amount describes to what extent the test objects misbehave on each source video and its followup video(s). And considering that the number of mapped frame pairs varies among different source videos, we report the ratio of the mapped frames with inconsistence detected when using different source videos. And for the results with the four MRs that generate five follow-up videos for every source video, we report the average ratio with every source video.

According to the results in Table II, we first found that the three test objects make tracking errors in much more frames under MR1-1 than under the other four MRs. Considering that MR1-1 simulates a stable speed variety for the tracked objects, this demonstrates that the speed variety of tracked objects can make the test objects fail to track some objects in much time. And with the source videos Nos. 00, 08, 13, and 27, at least one test object cannot correctly track some objects in over half the time. This finding conforms with the real-life situation that we introduce in Section II-B, i.e., current MOT systems can be sensitive to the speed of tracked objects . They may fail to track the objects moving at diverse speeds and even cause fatal incidents. It reminds us to seriously consider the robustness of MOT systems against the speed variety of tracked objects.

Compared to MR1-1, the other four MRs that simulate some occasional temporary changes make the test objects misbehave in relatively less time. However, such slight changes can still lead to many tracking errors (in the tests whose ratio is greater than zero). This demonstrates these test objects are unable to immediately recover from the temporary invalid frame and correctly track those objects in subsequent normal frames . Furthermore, we notice that the test objects misbehave in over 1% frames in many tests (whose ratios are NOT shown as italic gray values ). Recall that these MRs merely modify 1% frames in the source video. This finding demonstrates that modifying a number of frames can have the test objects make errors on a greater number of unchanged frames. This reminds that the effect of a short-time disturbance can be quite far-reaching . That is, the occasional invalid content in a frame can mislead the tracking on more than its subsequent one frame .

Besides, in MR1-2, MR2-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3, we found that MR2-2 and MR2-3 trigger tracking errors on slightly more frames compared to MR1-2 and MR2-2. Consider that MR2-2 and MR2-3 disturb (i.e., pixelate and blur) the content in some frames; while MR1-2 and MR2-1 solely remove or cover some frames without disturbing and adding noise to the frames. This demonstrates that the test objects are fairly more vulnerable to the noise disturbance than to the slight information loss .

Next, we analyze the test results at error level . Specifically, we report and analyze the numbers of detected errors in three types. As a reminder, the numbers of the errors detected with distinct source videos present a similar tendency with that on the ratios, which has been discussed above. Thus, with limited space, we do not separately report the number with each source video as above. And for MR1-2, MR2-1, MR2-2, and MR2-3, here we also report the average result on five follow-up videos.

Table III presents the results. For different scenarios (MRs), we found that the performance of the test objects is also with a similar tendency as we observe on the ratios above. That is, the test objects make much more errors (in every type) against the stable speed variety, which is simulated by MR1-1, than the temporary camera failures simulated by the other four MRs. And in those four MRs, three test objects are more struggling to MR2-2 and MR2-3, which disturb the image content, than MR1-2 and MR2-2, which make some information lost.

When comparing the numbers of detected errors in different types, we found that for SORT+YOLOv3 and CenterTrack, the most errors are about the missing detection. This demonstrates that the limited robustness of these two test objects in diverse scenarios is usually blamed for missing to detect the tracked objects that can be detected in the source video . (It is worth noting that the object detection errors of MOT systems are not totally blamed for their integrated object detection systems, as some MOT systems will refine the output of the object detector during the association [16], [32]. Thus, it is still necessary and vital to study the errors in the final object detection results for MOT.) This finding suggests that these two test objects tend to be non-robust and would miss a few objects when the scenario changes. Meanwhile, when some objects are correctly detected by these two test objects, they are usually associated with the The style of a value indicates its range: bold red values are in (0.5, 1.0]; blue values are in (0.05, 0.5]; normal values are in (0.01, 0.05]; italic gray values are in [0, 0.01].

## C. Performance Comparison Among Test Objects (RQ3)

In RQ1 and RQ2, we investigate the general findings on the three test objects based on our test results at three granularities. In this RQ, we turn to the comparison among the performance of test objects and discuss their respective pros and cons based on our test results. Consider that based on the video level test results in Table I, the test objects have a similar performance in general. In this RQ, we compare the performance of three test objects based on the frame and error-level test results. For simplicity, SORT+YOLOv3, PointTrack, and CenterTrack are referred as 'S.+Y.', 'P.T.', and 'C.T.' in this section.

We first compare the performance among three test objects with the test results at frame level . From Table II, we found that the performance tendency among three test objects can be summarized into three groups that involve different scenarios.

Group 1 is about the stable speed variety of tracked objects. Only MR1-1 belongs to this group of scenario. In this scenario, S.+Y. misbehaves in the greatest amount of frames. This tells that S.+Y. is with the worst robustness against the stable speed variety of tracked objects. Nevertheless, P.T. and C.T. also do

## not express good robustness. This reminds us to improve such robustness for all three test objects, notably for S.+Y. .

Group 2 is about the information loss in few frames, which consists of MR1-2 and MR2-1. In this scenario, C.T. presents the best robustness in general. We consider the reason is C.T. jointly detects and tracks objects with one model [32], thus its two functions might help each other defend against the slight information loss. Meanwhile, P.T. shows the worst robustness. This may be because P.T. associates all the objects detected by its instance segmentation model without any refinement during the association phase [27]. This tells a mutual bind between detection and association may benefit the MOT robustness .

Group 3 is about adding occasional noise on image content, which is made up of MR2-2 and MR2-3. In this scenario, S.+Y. presents the best robustness. P.T. still makes many errors. But unlike under Group 2 , C.T. struggles here. Actually, S.+Y. also refines the output of its object detector during association, but S.+Y. makes the bind between these two steps less tight since it completes them by adopting two different modules [16]. This may assist one module in retaining good robustness when the other is impaired, thus benefiting the robustness of the whole MOT system. In comparison, C.T. employs a joint model to solve the two steps simultaneously [32]. With such a tight bind between two steps, the two functions of this model could be vulnerable to quite similar patterns. This will make the whole MOT system hardly recover when facing these patterns. This outcome further suggests the bind between two steps should be appropriate , which supplements the previous inspiration.

Next, we further supplement some unique findings based on the test results at error level . From the results in Table III, one of the most striking points should be that we have not detected any inconsistence error regarding object detection for P.T. This demonstrates that P.T. can always detect consistent objects in diverse scenarios simulated by our MRs. In fact, this is within our expectation. As mentioned above, P.T. does not change the object detection results returned by its instance segmentation model. Thus, it always gives robust object detection results on the unchanged frames. But the consistence on object detection does not make the final tracking results of P.T. robust. Quite a few errors on object association are identified for P.T. and the total number of tracking errors of P.T. is also greater than the other two test objects on many MRs. This again suggests the importance of one appropriate relation between the object detection and association . In addition, we found S.+Y. makes fairly fewer errors regarding both the object detection and the object association against the noise disturbance introduced by MR2-2 and MR2-3. This suggests a possibility to improve the robustness of MOT systems against the noise disturbance by learning from S.+Y.. In fact, our test results suggest different MOT systems have their own pros and cons, thus, it should be beneficial to make them learn from each other for win-win .

## D. Error-Prone Scenes of Test Objects (RQ4)

As we discuss in RQ2, we found these test objects make much more tracking errors on some video pairs than the other videos. Considering different video pairs are of different road scenes [47], we conjecture that in some scenes the test objects are more apt to be less robust . Thus, in this RQ, we manually review the detected tracking errors, notably on the video pairs where the test objects make more errors, to summarize some error-prone scenes. Finally, we identify the two most common scenes that cover about 50% and 30% of the identified errors, respectively. Here we illustrate these two typical scenes with some intuitive examples where the test objects misbehave on a frame that is just after one changed frame. We also present two precedent frames to clearly illustrate the errors of ID switch.

## · Scene 1: Tracking Objects Being Partially Covered.

The first representative scene where the test objects behave less robustly is that the tracked objects densely overlap with each other. S1E1 and S1E2 in Fig. 5 are the examples for this scene. In S1E1, several cars are densely parked on both sides of the road. After a blurred frame f i -1 , three cars are missed in f i . And in S1E2, a car that is partially covered by another car is associated into two distinct trajectories (indicated by the change in the color of its mask). In fact, we found the actual error is with the ID assignment on this car in the source video (masked in purple in f j -2 but orange in f j ). This demonstrates that our method can detect the tracking errors on not only the follow-up video, but also the source video.

## · Scene 2: Tracking Objects with a Small Size.

The other representative scene where the test objects behave less robustly is that the tracked objects are with a small size. S2E1 and S2E2 in Fig. 5 are the corresponding examples. In S2E1, after removing a frame to simulate the speed up of the small-sized car being tracked, this car cannot be tracked in the subsequent f i . And in S2E2, f i -1 is covered with f j -2 so as to simulate a short-time video freeze. Without the information in f j -1 that should have been presented in f i -1 , an ID switch is present on the tracking result of a car with a small size.

We consider both two scenes are essential and common in the daily use of MOT systems. In fact, practitioners may have noticed that these scenes are challenging to MOT systems and prepared test cases (e.g., our source videos) of these scenes to evaluate MOT systems. Current MOT systems have also shown a fairly good performance on these test cases (according to the relatively pleasing accuracy in benchmark-based evaluations). However, our method generates new cases of these scenes and reveals several MOT systems may still struggle with these scenes in some scenarios , such as the speed of tracked objects varying and camera temporarily failing. Based on this, we suggest the practitioners to consider further improving the robustness of MOT systems in these scenes.

## VI. T HREATS TO V ALIDITY

The first threat to validity is about the representativeness of the dataset and test objects used in our evaluation. To counter this threat, we use a widely-adopted MOT dataset that consists of 29 videos of real-world road scenes captured by the onboard camera of running cars. These test cases are similar to the ones that can be easily obtained in the daily usage of MOT systems in terms of content and collection access. And the test objects in our evaluation are all typical representatives of mainstream categories of MOT systems. Thus, our evaluation setup should be representative. We also plan to evaluate our method on the other MOT systems and datasets in our future work.

The second threat to validity is that we have only considered two scenarios and designed five MRs, which have not covered all the MOT scenarios. It is true that this may cause missing of some robustness defects. But no existing studies have claimed their MRs are complete since there is no criterion for the completeness of MRs. In fact, this is the fundamental limitation of testing, that is, we can never detect all the defects by testing. In this work, we focus on two common and essential scenarios with five MRs and detect many actual issues. Thus, our results should be representative and meaningful. And we will also try to design new MRs to cover more scenarios in future.

The last threat to validity is on the parameters for our MRs. To simulate diverse specific scenarios about speed variety and camera failures, we design parameters to adjust the number of changed frames. In this paper, we try a typical setup to mimic the common 2x-speed-up of tracked objects (MR1-1) and four occasional disturbance on video (the other four MRs). We have carefully studied the characteristics of the test cases in KITTI, e.g., duration and car speeds, to ensure the follow-up test cases generated with these source test cases and specified parameters can mimic valid and real MOT scenarios to reveal actual MOT defects. During the real-life usage of our method, practitioners can adjust the parameters or try more settings according to the traits of their own source test cases to generate valid follow-up cases and assess the robustness of MOT systems in the other specific scenarios of speed variety and camera failure.

## VII. R ELATED W ORKS

## A. Robustness Testing For Visual Perception Systems

The first group of related works is on the robustness testing for visual perception systems. The existing works in this group majorly focus on the objection detection (OD) systems. Wang et al. [1] propose a method, MetaOD, to test OD systems with an MR to insert objects to the source images. It could also be seen as a method to test the robustness of OD systems in the scenario where the amount of objects varies. Next, researchers improve the reality of the inserted objects [2] or try to remove objects from the source images [3]. Yan et al. [48] adopt MRs that simulate the variety of brightness, color, and so on, to test the systems that detect texts in images. As these works are for OD, they majorly focus on the variety of static image content. Unlike them, our work tests MOT systems that perceive videos with multiple image frames. We propose five MRs particularly focusing on two dynamic features exclusive in MOT and reveal several robustness defects, some of which may have not been detected with existing MRs and aware by the community.

(d) Scene 2 Example 2 (abbr. S2E2, detected by MR2-1)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Fig. 5: Examples for Two Typical Error-Prone Scenes of Test Objects

There are also a few works studying the robustness of visual perception systems against Adversarial Examples (AEs). Some works add certain specifc perturbations to images to formulate AEs and mislead OD systems on these images [49]-[52]. And some studies have also investigated the AEs for MOT systems. They add particular artificial noise to different videos, aiming to mislead MOT systems in tracking the objects in the frames after the changed frames [6], [53]. Our method also reasonably follows such works to check the tracking results on unchanged frames. But compared to all these studies about AEs, our work focuses on the robustness issues in common real-life scenarios, whose samples would not contain deliberate artificial noise.

Overall, as mentioned in Section II-B, our MRs supplement the current MRs by filling the blank of robustness evaluation in the real scenarios involving the changes on dynamic features, thus promote the extensive test for visual perception systems.

## B. Robustness Testing For Autonomous Driving

One of the most popular safety-critical applications of MOT systems is autonomous driving (AD). Apart from the MOT and ODsystems, several studies have investigated the robustness of the other AD modules in various scenarios. Some of them test if the image-based steering decision modules can robustly give consistent decisions in scenarios with different brightness and noise [54], distinct weather [8], [55], and disturbed billboards [56]. There are also a few works on the robustness of LiDARbased perceptual modules. They add various noise to the point cloud data collected by sensors and test whether the LiDARbased object detection systems can keep the correct detection [57]-[59]. But these works also mainly focus on the robustness of AD modules in the scenarios that solely involve the variety of static features. Besides, there are also some studies testing the robustness of the whole AD system on several simulation platforms [60], [61] and in the field [60], [62]. However, none of them has tested the robustness of MOT systems, which are also vital in AD. In this paper, we preliminarily fill this blank. And we believe the revealed MOT defects can be meaningful to inspiring the improvement on AD robustness and reliability.

## VIII. C ONCLUSION AND F UTURE W ORK

Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) systems are broadly-used in many safety-critical applications that track objects in video, such as autonomous driving. The robustness defects of MOT systems may disturb these applications and harm public safety. In this paper, we propose the first method to efficiently test the robustness of MOT systems in the scenarios that involve speed variety of tracked objects and temporary camera failures. We leverage it to test three typical MOT systems and successfully reveal many robustness defects for them. We also extensively discuss their performance based on our test results, as well as summarize two representative scenes where they often fail. In future, we will use our method to test other MOT systems with more data. And we also plan to design MRs on new scenarios to further extensively evaluate the robustness of MOT systems.
